--- Page 1 ---
Quantifying the hosting capacity value of workload flexibility for AI data centers: A
two-stage electricity–computation co-optimization framework
Jiakai Wua, Pengyu Rena, Yifan Wanga, Wei Suna,∗
aSchool of Engineering, The University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh EH9 3FB, Scotland, United Kingdom
Abstract
Grid connection constraints increasingly limit the expansion of AI-era data centers, yet the additional hosting capacity enabled
by computational workload flexibility remains insufficiently quantified. This paper develops a two-stage electricity–computation
co-optimization framework to quantify the individual and coordinated hosting capacity values of spatial and temporal workload
flexibility. Data center capacities are determined endogenously, with computational task arrivals scaling with admitted capacity.
Spatial routing of eligible interactive requests and temporal deferral of batch workloads are linked to server operation and facility
power demand, subject to workload completion requirements and transmission constraints. The first stage maximizes aggregate
hosting capacity; the second fixes the resulting site capacities and optimizes annual workload scheduling and generation dispatch to
minimize generation and carbon costs. An 8760-hour case study with three data centers on a modified IEEE 118-bus system shows
that temporal and spatial flexibility individually increase hosting capacity by 21.26% and 5.37%, respectively. Their coordinated
use raises hosting capacity from 4635.1 MW to 6231.5 MW, a 34.44% increase without network reinforcement. The coordinated
gain exceeds the sum of the individual gains by 361.9 MW, demonstrating complementarity between spatial migration and temporal
deferral. By redistributing computational demand across locations and operating hours, these mechanisms enable fuller utilization
of existing transmission capacity. The findings establish workload flexibility as a quantifiable planning resource for accommodating
additional data center capacity within existing transmission networks.
Keywords: AI Data centers, Electricity-computation co-optimization, Hosting capacity, Workload flexibility, Transmission
congestion
1. Introduction
1.1. Background and motivation
Driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and continued dig-
itization, data centers (DCs) are emerging as one of the
fastest-growing and most concentrated sources of electricity
demand. Global DC electricity consumption reached approx-
imately 415 TWh in 2024 and is projected to more than dou-
ble to around 945 TWh by 2030, with AI expected to drive the
largest share of this increase [1]. In the United States, DCs ac-
counted for approximately 4.4% of national electricity in 2023,
and this share is projected to reach 6.7–12% by 2028 [2]. At
the project level, new hyper-scale facilities are being devel-
oped with connection capacities of 100-1000 MW, and utili-
ties are receiving individual connection requests of 1 GW or
more [3]. NERC further reports that emerging large loads range
from multi-megawatt facilities to multi-gigawatt complexes re-
quiring transmission level connections and associated network
upgrades [4]. These developments concentrate substantial de-
mand at individual points of interconnection and within a lim-
ited number of regional clusters. Consequently, the local net-
work impact of an AI-era DC can be considerably greater than
∗Corresponding author.
Email addresses: s2902684@ed.ac.uk (Jiakai Wu),
s2192464@ed.ac.uk (Pengyu Ren), s2154060@ed.ac.uk (Yifan Wang),
w.sun@ed.ac.uk (Wei Sun)
its contribution to national annual electricity consumption. Al-
though improvements in hardware efficiency and server utiliza-
tion have moderated historical growth in DC electricity con-
sumption [5], they do not reduce the need to supply increas-
ingly large blocks of connection capacity at specific network
locations.
The rapid development cycle of DCs further intensifies this
locational challenge. New hyper-scale capacity can potentially
be developed within one to two years, while a typical DC can
become operational within two to three years [3]. By com-
parison, new transmission infrastructure typically requires four
to eight years to develop in advanced economies, while lead
times for critical equipment such as transformers and cables
have also lengthened [1]. In established European DC hubs,
grid connection times can extend to ten years because of net-
work congestion and the need for substantial grid reinforcement
[6]. This mismatch means that a DC project may be ready for
operation well before the fundamental electricity infrastructure
required for its requested connection. Consequently, grid con-
straints could delay approximately 20% of the global DC capac-
ity planned for deployment by 2030 [1]. The relevant planning
question is whether the existing network can accommodate the
proposed DC capacity at the requested connection point and
target date. For an existing network, this capacity is further
constrained by the transmission headroom available across the

operating hours in which DC demand coincides with other sys-
tem demand. DC hosting capacity is thus inherently dependent
on both spatial connection location and temporal operational
conditions.
Under a conventional firm connection, the demand profile as-
sociated with the proposed DC connection capacity must re-
main feasible with respect to network operating constraints
across all operating hours. The resulting HC may therefore be
constrained by a small number of congested node-hour combi-
nations, even when transmission headroom remains available at
other locations or times. Workload flexibility provides a means
of coordinating DC electricity demand with these spatially and
temporally varying network conditions. Previous research has
demonstrated that dispatchable computing loads can improve
grid utilization by relocating computational demand [7]. For
DCs, this coordination begins with the computational service:
facility electricity demand is determined by the workloads pro-
cessed through IT equipment and the power required by cool-
ing and other supporting systems [8]. Latency-sensitive inter-
active requests can be routed among geographically distributed
DCs, whereas delay-tolerant batch workloads can be deferred
within prescribed completion windows. These scheduling de-
cisions change server utilization and facility power demand
while preserving the associated computing service. Fleet-scale
implementations have further demonstrated the practical feasi-
bility of temporal workload scheduling across geographically
distributed computing resources [9]. This coupling motivates
an electricity-computation co-optimization framework in which
workload scheduling, DC power consumption, power system
operation, and transmission feasibility are represented consis-
tently.
Within this framework, the value of DC flexibility
in hosting capacity is quantified as the additional network-
constrained HC enabled relative to an inflexible DC workload
configuration.
1.2. Literature review and research gap
Research on DC flexibility has evolved along three connected
directions: modeling the computational sources of DC flexible
power demand, coordinating that demand with power system
operation, and assessing DC siting and hosting capacity. Ta-
ble 1 compares the studies most directly related to network-
constrained DC hosting capacity assessment.
The compari-
son distinguishes the representation of DC power demand, the
available workload flexibility dimensions, the scale and config-
uration of the DC portfolio, the modeled network constraints,
and the treatment of connection capacity. The final column
identifies whether flexibility is valued through the additional
HC enabled by DC workload scheduling.
The first research direction establishes the computational ba-
sis of flexible DC power demand. Workload-to-power formu-
lations translate the allocation and execution of computational

tasks into server activation, utilization, and facility power con-
sumption, enabling spatial and temporal scheduling to be rep-
resented within power system operation [10, 13, 16]. Data-
driven methods complement these formulations by estimating
the deferrable power associated with periodic batch workloads
from operational traces [11].
The amount of available flex-
ibility depends on the service characteristics of the underly-
ing workloads. QoS-aware demand response studies show that
job scheduling and server level power control can provide grid
response while maintaining computing service requirements
[21]. Trace-driven analysis across interactive and batch work-
loads further demonstrates that the available temporal and spa-
tial shifting depend on job duration, completion deadlines, ser-
vice level objectives, and the available destination regions [22].
Workload flexibility is therefore a service-constrained capabil-
ity defined by the extent to which computation can be shifted
across locations and time while satisfying its service require-
ments.
The second direction incorporates this capability into power
system coordination. Virtual-link formulations represent tem-
poral deferral and spatial migration as non-physical transfer
pathways in network-constrained market clearing, allowing
their effects on nodal prices and system operation to be evalu-
ated [12]. Related incentive mechanisms coordinate the spatial-
temporal response of DCs with power system requirements
[23], while detailed electricity-computation models schedule
heterogeneous workloads under network and uncertainty con-
straints [16]. These capabilities have been applied to renewable
energy matching and carbon-aware operation [24, 25], trans-
mission and server planning [26], balancing and non-wire al-
ternatives [27], post-fault restoration [28], and distribution net-
work congestion management [29]. Collectively, these stud-
ies demonstrate how workload scheduling changes the location
and time of DC power demand and produces measurable op-
erational, economic, and environmental outcomes. Their as-
sessments generally begin from a prescribed DC portfolio or
determine DC capacity through cost, carbon, or investment ob-
jectives; the maximum hosting capacity supported by workload
flexibility is not their principal assessment quantity.
The third direction moves from system operation to DC
siting, sizing, and interconnection capacity.
Joint planning
models make DC location and capacity endogenous along-
side electricity-system investment and operation [14, 15].
Flexibility-aware connection screening evaluates whether GW-
scale projects can be accommodated at candidate locations un-
der firm, pause, and shift envelopes [17]. Explicit HC formula-
tions have also quantified the admissible DC loads supported by
batteries, dispatchable generation, and reactive power resources
in distribution networks [18]. At the transmission level, recent
studies assess feasible allocations of multiple DCs under con-
tingency requirements [19] and examine how electrolyzers can
support AI-training DCs subject to voltage and frequency con-
straints [20]. These studies bring DC power demand directly
into network-capacity assessment. Flexible demand is typically
represented through prescribed DC power envelopes or load
profiles, or provided by additional flexibility resources, rather
than being endogenously derived from computational work-
loads whose processing is scheduled across locations and time.
Taken together, the existing literature leaves the relationship
between workload flexibility and network hosting capacity in-
sufficiently resolved. A hosting capacity-centered assessment
should simultaneously make the capacities of multiple DCs en-
dogenous and preserve workload completion under spatial and
temporal scheduling under transmission network constraints. It
must also evaluate comparable flexibility configurations on the
same network so that differences in hosting capacity can be
attributed directly to workload flexibility. Such a formulation
makes it possible to quantify not only the additional DC ca-
pacity enabled by flexibility, but also the workload adjustments
and network operating conditions through which these hosting
capacity gains are realized.
1.3. Research questions and contributions
The literature review identifies two complementary research
strands. Electricity-computation coordination studies have es-
tablished how spatial and temporal workload scheduling can
improve the operation of a DC portfolio, while hosting capac-
ity studies have quantified the connection capacity of electric-
ity networks under static or exogenously prescribed DC power
demand. Connecting these two strands requires a framework
3


--- Page 4 ---
that makes multiple DC hosting capacities endogenous, derives
their power demand from computational workloads, and quanti-
fies workload flexibility through the additional hosting capacity
it enables. This forms the central focus of the present study. Ac-
cordingly, this paper addresses three research questions. First,
how much aggregate DC hosting capacity can a transmission
network accommodate? Second, how much additional host-
ing capacity is enabled by spatial and temporal flexibility indi-
vidually, and how does their coordination change these gains?
Third, how is the DC flexibility activated across locations and
time, and how does this activation affect network operation to
support additional hosting capacity? To answer these questions,
the main contributions are as follows:
1. An electricity-computation co-optimization model is de-
veloped for assessing the hosting capacity of multiple DCs
connected to a transmission network. The hosting capac-
ity of each DC determines its computational task arrivals,
which are mapped through workload scheduling, server
operation, and DC power demand seen by the network.
2. A two-stage optimization framework is formulated that
connects the planning value of workload flexibility with
network operation. The framework first determines the
maximum aggregate DC hosting capacity, and subse-
quently optimizes annual workload scheduling and power
system operation at the resulting capacity allocation. This
provides a unified assessment of how much DC hosting
capacity is enabled by flexibility and how these gains
are realized through coordinated workload scheduling and
power system operation.
3. The mechanism through which DC workload flexibility
enables additional hosting capacity is characterized. Spa-
tial migration and temporal deferral align DC power de-
mand with available network headroom across locations
and time. By separating the individual contributions of
spatial and temporal flexibility from the interaction ef-
fect, the analysis reveals how workload scheduling con-
verts available network headroom into DC hosting capac-
ity.
These contributions extend ECC from the operational use of
a given DC portfolio to the planning question of how much ca-
pacity a fixed network can credibly host. They also provide a
service-preserving basis for valuing computational flexibility in
flexible or non-firm connection assessments.
1.4. Paper organization
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion 2 develops the DC power, IT equipment, and workload
management models. Section 3 formulates the problem state-
ment and develops the proposed two-stage hosting capacity as-
sessment framework. Section 4 defines the hosting capacity
value metrics and introduces the study system, experimental
settings, comparative results, flexibility activation mechanisms,
and system impact analysis. Section 5 summarizes the conclu-
sions, planning implications, and priorities for future work.
2. Modeling of data center power and workload manage-
ment
This section develops a model of DC power consumption
and workload scheduling. DC power consumption is jointly
determined by the computational tasks processed through IT
equipment and the electricity required by cooling and other
facility-support systems. Among these components, IT equip-
ment and cooling systems account for the majority of DC power
consumption, with IT equipment representing the largest share
[30]. Therefore, accurately modeling the power-consumption
characteristics of computation is fundamental to constructing
a comprehensive DC power model. The formulation connects
three interdependent layers: workload scheduling, server opera-
tion, and DC power consumption. Workload arrivals scale with
the DC hosting capacity and are divided into interactive, batch,
and inflexible components. The workload processed at different
locations and times determines active-server requirements and
utilization, which are mapped to IT power and subsequently to
total DC power demand. This workload-to-power model pro-
vides the DC-side foundation for the methodology developed
in Section 3.
2.1. Data center power modeling
The total power demand of a DC comprises IT power and the
power required by cooling and other facility-support systems.
These non-IT requirements are represented in aggregate using
a fixed power usage effectiveness (PUE), denoted by ηDC [2].
The relationship between IT power and total facility power is
expressed as:
pDC

demand, including cooling, lighting and other facility-support
loads. Thus, changes in IT power caused by workload schedul-
ing are translated into changes in the total DC power demand
supplied by the network.
2.2. IT equipment modeling
IT power consumption is modeled as a function of the num-
ber of active servers and their utilization [31]. Let mn,t denote
the continuous equivalent number of active servers at DC n in
period t, and let un,t denote their average utilization. The power
consumption of an active server increases linearly from its idle
power pidle

links the scheduled workload and active-server requirement to
IT power.
2.3. Workload modeling
Workload flexibility is represented through three classes with
different processing requirements. Interactive workloads can be
routed among eligible DCs for processing within the same pe-
riod, whereas batch workloads can be deferred within a pre-
scribed completion window at their original DC. Inflexible
workloads must be processed at their original location and time.
In all cases, workload arrivals scale with admitted DC ca-
pacity, so that additional hosting capacity carries an additional
computing service obligation.
The workload arrival is ex-
pressed as:

locations and time.
2.3.1. Interactive workloads
Interactive workloads are subject to strict latency require-
ments. However, eligible task requests can be routed to other
eligible DCs for processing, providing spatial flexibility.

each hour.
2.3.2. Batch workloads
Batch workloads comprise delay-tolerant computational
tasks, including AI training and data-management tasks, that
can be completed within prescribed time windows. Deferring
eligible batch workloads within these windows allows DCs to
redistribute computing demand across time, providing temporal
flexibility.

3. Hosting capacity assessment methodology
3.1. Problem statement
The mismatch between DC development and grid expan-
sion timelines means that the network may not expand quickly
enough to accommodate all proposed DC connections. Har-
vesting the flexibility within DCs therefore offers a potential
solution for accommodating additional DC capacity through
more effective use of the existing network capacity. Against this
background, the problem considered in this paper is to quantify
the maximum DC hosting capacity that can be connected to the
transmission network. Each MW of admitted DC capacity is
associated with a corresponding volume of computational task
arrivals. Feasible hosting capacity must therefore support the
complete computing service obligation over the annual hori-
zon. The resulting hosting capacity represents the maximum
compute-backed DC hosting capacity that can be accommo-
dated by the network [18].
To achieve electricity-computation co-optimization,
the
problem is formulated from a coordinated system planning per-
spective.
Fig. 1 illustrates the coupling between DC work-
load management and power system operation.
On the DC
side, interactive workloads may be migrated among geograph-
ically distributed DCs, providing spatial flexibility, while batch
workloads may be deferred within service windows, providing
temporal flexibility. The scheduled workload at each DC de-
termines IT power consumption and, consequently, total DC
power demand. On the power system side, DC power demand
enters the nodal power balance and affects generation, voltage
angles, and transmission flows.
3.2. Proposed two-stage framework
3.2.1. Framework overview
The proposed framework adopts a sequential lexicographic
structure that assigns distinct planning functions to hosting ca-
pacity assessment and system operational optimization. The
two stages therefore follow the sequence of first determining
how much DC hosting capacity can be connected and where it
can be accommodated, and then determining how the resulting
DC portfolio and power system should be operated.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, the DC hosting capacity vector
H⋆
c provides the coupling between the two stages. This two-
stage structure provides complementary planning and opera-
tional outputs. Differences in the Stage 1 frontiers across flex-
ibility configurations quantify the individual and coordinated
hosting capacity values of spatial and temporal workload flex-
ibility. The corresponding Stage 2 solutions reveal how flex-
ibility is deployed across DCs and operating hours, and how
the resulting DC power demand redistribution influences gen-
eration and transmission network conditions. The framework
therefore connects the hosting capacity value of DC flexibility
with the operational mechanisms.
3.2.2. Stage 1: hosting capacity assessment
Stage 1 determines the DC capacities and workload sched-
ules and is formulated as follows:

The Stage 2 objective in Eq. (28) optimizes system opera-
tion at the hosting capacity frontier by minimizing total system
operational cost. It combines the quadratic conventional gener-
ation cost in Eq. (30) with the explicit carbon cost in Eq. (31),
thereby considering the emissions associated with dispatch and
favoring lower carbon supply [32]. The resulting solution de-
scribes cost-minimizing annual operation for the capacity allo-
cation obtained in Stage 1.
3.2.4. Compact two-stage formulation
Following the detailed stage formulations, the complete lex-
icographic structure is written in the hierarchical form of
Eq. (32). The framework first maximizes aggregate DC host-
ing capacity and then minimizes annual operating cost at the
7

Both stages are subject to the DC power and IT constraints
in Eqs. (1)–(3), the workload conservation and completion
constraints in Eqs. (6)–(16), the DC connection constraint in
Eq. (19), and the generation and transmission-network con-
straints in Eqs. (20)–(27). The generation and carbon costs are
defined in Eqs. (30) and (31), respectively.
This sequential procedure gives priority to hosting capacity
maximization and then minimizes operating cost for the opti-
mized DC hosting capacity.
4. Case studies
This section evaluates the proposed framework on a modi-
fied IEEE-118 transmission network. The models were imple-
mented in Julia 1.12.5 and solved using Gurobi 13.0.0 [33]. All
computations were executed on a workstation equipped with a
14-core Intel Core i7 CPU @2.30 GHz and 16 GB RAM.
4.1. Experiment settings
The study uses a modified IEEE-118 transmission system,
whose source provides annual network, generator, load, wind,
and solar data [34]. Fig. 2 summarizes the modified transmis-
sion network and the prospective DC locations. The system
contains 118 buses and 186 lines, with DCs connected at buses
32, 78, and 90. All simulations are conducted over an 8760-
hour year with a 1-hour resolution.
Workload arrival profiles are derived from the IN2P3 2024
Workload Dataset [35]. Based on [36] and characteristics of DC
workloads, the shares of interactive, batch, and fixed workloads
are assumed to be 40%, 20%, and 40% respectively (Fig. 3).
The DC configuration parameters are listed in Table 2, based
on [37, 38].
Table 2: Configuration of DCs.
Parameter
Value
ηDC
1.20

1.3 (kW)
ppeak
1.9 (kW)

¯U
0.80
T D
6 (h)
To quantify the hosting capacity value of DC workload flex-
ibility, the following four cases are simulated and compared:
• Case 1: No workload flexibility (NF).
• Case 2: Temporal flexibility of batch workloads (TF).
• Case 3: Spatial flexibility of interactive workloads (SF).
• Case 4: Coordinated spatial and temporal workload flexi-
bility (STF).
4.2. Simulation results analysis
Fig. 4 compares the annual DC power profiles under the four
flexibility configurations. Case 2 broadly preserves the con-
sumption pattern of each DC in Case 1, while reshaping the
temporal profile as batch workloads can be deferred within their
allowable window. Case 3 exhibits a distinct spatial redistribu-
tion pattern: DC1 and DC2 consume less power than case 1
over long periods, whereas DC3 accommodates a larger share
of workload. Case 4 combines these patterns with particularly
pronounced high-power periods at DC3. Importantly, the dif-
ferences among the trajectories reflect both the larger work-
load scale enabled by the increased hosting capacity and the
optimized spatial or temporal scheduling. The corresponding
workload migration and deferral volumes are examined in Sec-
tion 4.3.
The following metrics quantify the hosting capacity gains
relative to different cases. Case 1 (NF) serves as the benchmark
for the other cases. The absolute and relative hosting capacity
gains are defined as:

HCCEc =

Table 3 establishes Case 1 as the inflexible benchmark, with
an aggregated hosting capacity of 4635.1 MW. Enabling tempo-
ral flexibility alone in Case 2 raises this frontier to 5620.5 MW,
corresponding to a gain of 985.4 MW (21.26% improvement
over case 1). Spatial flexibility alone increases HC by 249.1
MW (5.37%), raising the frontier to 4884.2 MW. The coordi-
nated temporal and spatial flexibility in Case 4 achieves the
largest hosting capacity, 6231.5 MW, which is 1596.4 MW
(34.44% above the benchmark). This result reflects the greater
flexibility value of temporal deferral, which can shift work-
load away from network-constrained hours and exploit head-
room available in subsequent periods, whereas spatial shifting
is limited to the headroom available at alternative DC locations
within the same hour. Coordinating the two mechanisms pro-
duces the largest HC gain in this case study.

Substituting the results reported in Table 3 into Eq. (35) gives
VHC
interaction = 361.9 MW, equivalent to 7.81% of the Case 1 fron-
tier. The coordinated HC gain therefore exceeds the sum of the
two individual gains by 361.9 MW. Equivalently, adding spatial
flexibility to the temporally flexible case yields an additional
611.0 MW of HC, whereas adding temporal flexibility to the
spatially flexible case yields a further 1347.3 MW. This pos-
itive interaction indicates that temporal and spatial flexibility
are complementary in expanding the feasible hosting capacity
region, rather than providing merely additive benefits.
Fig. 5 compares the hosting capacity of the three DCs across
the four cases. Under Case 1, DC3 receives the largest HC, ap-
proximately 2498 MW, compared with 1231 MW at DC1 and
906 MW at DC2. Temporal flexibility in Case 2 increases the
HC assigned to all three DCs. Spatial flexibility in Case 3 in-
stead reshapes the allocation: more HC is supported at DC1
while the HC at DC3 is lower than in Case 1, but the aggre-
gate HC of the three DCs still increases. Under coordinated
temporal and spatial flexibility, the HC at DC1 and DC2 rise to
approximately 2033 and 1809 MW, respectively, while DC3 re-
tains approximately 2389 MW. Relative to Case 1, the increases
at DC1 and DC2 therefore more than compensate for the mod-
est reduction at DC3. This reallocation represents the optimiza-
tion outcome through which flexibility redistributes the addi-
tional hosting capacity across DC locations.
The system operational costs reported in Table 3 should be
interpreted separately for each case, as each value corresponds
to the hosting capacity frontier of the respective case. Relative

to Case 1, Cases 2–4 support more hosting capacity and have
higher annual costs, reaching £4.546, £4.442, and £4.641 bil-
lion, respectively. The corresponding HCCE values, calculated
from the cost, remain within a range of 6.77–6.99 MW per mil-
lion pounds. Case 4 thus delivers the largest absolute HC gain,
although its incremental capacity-to-cost ratio is slightly lower
than those of Cases 2 and 3. The richer flexibility formulations
also increase computational complexity, resulting in longer so-
lution times, from 1190.15 s in Case 1 to 3167.51 s in Case 4.
These results quantify the HC frontier and its operational con-
sequence. The associated changes in network operation are ex-
amined in Section 4.4.
4.3. Analysis of flexibility in DCs
The HC gains reported in Section 4.2 raise a further question:
how is the available DC flexibility actually utilized in the oper-
ational schedule? Figure 6 addresses this question by showing
the actual spatial and temporal workload shifting in Case 4. The
widespread colored regions in Figs. 6(a) and (b) demonstrate
that both spatial and temporal flexibility are activated through-
out the year. The two maps therefore illustrate how spatial and
temporal flexibility reshape the location and time of DC power
demand in the optimized schedule.
The annual pattern of spatial flexibility in Fig. 6(a) has a clear
directional structure. DC1 and DC2 predominantly exhibit neg-
ative workload shifts, whereas DC3 experiences positive shifts,
with the spatial redistribution becoming more pronounced in
the later part of the year. The simultaneous occurrence of op-
posite signs across the three sites is consistent with workload
migration: DC1 and DC2 primarily act as workload-sending
DC sites, whereas DC3 predominantly serves as the workload-
receiving DC site. The persistence of this pattern across the
annual map shows that spatial flexibility is used as a recurring
portfolio-level response, although its intensity varies with date
and hour.
The annual pattern of temporal flexibility in Fig. 6(b) exhibits
a distinct operational pattern.
Each DC displays alternating
positive and negative regions, reflecting the temporal redistri-
bution of workload across the day. Overall, workload is mainly
shifted away from the morning and evening periods and to mid-
day and overnight hours. These shifts are unevenly distributed
across the year, and the late-year maps show more pronounced
variations, particularly at DC1 and DC3. Temporal flexibility
therefore reshapes DC power demand at each site, rather than
reproducing the redistribution across DCs observed for spatial
flexibility.

Fig. 6. Annual patterns of DC load shifting. a, b: Spatial and temporal load shifts under Case 4. Color mapping represents the quantity of net load shifts from other
DCs/other times (positive values) or shifts to other DCs/other times (negative values). c, d: Typical activation windows of spatial and temporal flexibility under
different cases.
The enlarged windows in Figs. 6(c) and (d) further highlight
these distinct spatial and temporal operating patterns. In the
September spatial window, the solid Case 4 profiles show an
increase at DC3 accompanied by reductions at DC1 and DC2.
The dashed SF profiles follow the same direction of shifting
but with smaller excursions over the main activated period. In
the November temporal window, the solid profiles alternate be-
tween negative and positive shifts at the three DCs, displaying
the deferral and subsequent recovery of workload within the
window. Relative to the dashed SF and TF profiles in panels (c)
and (d), respectively, the STF case modifies both the magnitude
and timing of the flexibility response at each DC, with the most
pronounced differences observed at DC1 and DC3.
Taken together, the annual maps and activation windows il-
lustrate how the two flexibility mechanisms complement each
other at the DC level. Spatial flexibility determines where eli-
gible workloads are processed, whereas temporal flexibility de-
termines when they are processed. Their coordinated utilization
therefore provides two distinct dimensions of adjustment in the
spatio-temporal scheduling of DC power demand. The result-
ing impacts on the power system are examined separately in the
next section.
4.4. Analysis of system impact
Sections 4.2 and 4.3 quantify the hosting capacity gains and
characterize the spatial and temporal workload shifting. This
section examines how workload shifting reshapes transmission
line loading and allows additional DC hosting capacity to be
accommodated within the existing network.
Fig. 7(a) illustrates the loading patterns of L41, L121, and
L140 during the selected peak period. Under Case 1 (NF), high
loading is particularly evident on L121 and L140 around the
middle of the period, while L41 exhibits more pronounced tem-
poral fluctuations. Under Case 2 (TF), near-limit loading on
L121 and L140 persists over a broader sequence of hours, re-
flecting how the larger volume of workload is accommodated
by scheduling its processing across time.
Case 3 (SF) pro-
duces a distinct spatial response: loading on L41 becomes more
sustained, whereas L140 experiences longer intervals of rela-
tively low loading. This redistribution demonstrates how shift-
ing workloads across DC locations reshapes transmission line
loading and alters the network headroom to accommodate ad-
ditional DC demand. Under Case 4 (STF), high line loading
extends to all three lines over a larger portion of the period.
Therefore, by scheduling DC power demand across time and
location, flexibility reshapes transmission line loading and en-
ables existing network headroom to be utilized more effectively.
The annual loading duration curves in Figs. 7(b)–(d) show
how these operational differences extend over the year. Case 4
(STF) exhibits the longest duration of near-limit operation on
all three transmission lines, indicating more sustained utiliza-
tion of their existing transmission capacity at the increased DC

Fig. 7. System impacts of data center flexibility under the four cases. a: Loading of critical lines (L41, L121, and L140) during the peak period. b, c, d: Annual

hosting capacity. The individual flexibility cases reveal distinct
responses. Relative to Case 1 (NF), Case 3 (SF) shortens near-
limit operation on L121 and extends it on L140, demonstrating
the redistribution of annual transmission line loading associated
with spatial flexibility. Case 2 (TF) extends near-limit operation
on all three lines through temporal flexibility. On L41, Case 2
(TF) also maintains elevated loading for longer at lower loading
thresholds. Temporal and spatial flexibility therefore produce
distinct annual loading patterns on the same transmission line
over the year.
Together, these results explain the network mechanism un-
derlying the hosting capacity gains. Spatial flexibility changes
the distribution of demand among DC locations, while temporal
flexibility changes its distribution across operating hours. Their
coordinated use provides additional ways to supply the growing
computational workload within the available transmission ca-
pacity. The more sustained loading observed under STF accom-
panies the increase in hosting capacity from 4635.1 MW under
NF to 6231.5 MW, corresponding to a 34.44% improvement re-
ported in Table 3. DC flexibility therefore increases the usable
network headroom for additional DC connection through coor-
dinated spatial and temporal scheduling of DC power demand.
5. Conclusions and future work
This paper developed a two-stage electricity–computation
co-optimization framework for quantifying the spatial and tem-
poral DC workload flexibility value in hosting capacity. The
framework integrates workload scheduling, DC power con-
sumption, generation dispatch, and transmission constraints
over a complete 8760-hour year.
The proposed two-stage
framework first identifies the maximum aggregate DC hosting
capacity in Stage 1 and then determines the annual system oper-
ation and DC workload schedule at the resulting hosting capac-
ity allocation in Stage 2. This formulation establishes a direct
connection between the planning value of DC flexibility and the
operational decisions through which that value is realized.
The modified IEEE-118 case study demonstrates that both
temporal and spatial workload flexibility increase the DC host-
ing capacity of the transmission network. Relative to the in-
flexible case, temporal and spatial flexibility provide gains of
985.4 MW (21.26%) and 249.1 MW (5.37%), respectively,
12


--- Page 13 ---
while their coordinated use increases the hosting capacity to
6231.5 MW, representing a gain of 1596.4 MW (34.44%). The
coordinated gain exceeds the sum of the stand-alone gains by
361.9 MW (7.81%), demonstrating the complementary value of
coordinated flexibility across locations and time. This value is
realized through distinct operational mechanisms: spatial flex-
ibility redirects interactive workloads primarily from DC1 and
DC2 to DC3, whereas temporal flexibility defers batch work-
loads from morning and evening periods to available midday
and overnight hours. Their coordinated activation consequently
reshapes both the hosting capacity allocation and the DC power
demand profile.
The resulting redistribution of line loading
among L41, L121, and L140, together with the longer dura-
tion of near-limit operation at the optimized hosting capacity,
indicates fuller utilization of the existing transmission network
capacity. Workload flexibility therefore enables the network to
accommodate additional DC hosting capacity by coordinating
where and when computational workloads are served.
Future work can extend the framework towards uncertainty-
aware connection assessment and its operational implemen-
tation.
Stochastic and distributionally robust optimization
can incorporate variations in computational task arrivals, con-
ventional system demand, and renewable availability to ob-
tain security and reliability-qualified hosting capacity values.
Matched capacity comparisons at a common DC hosting ca-
pacity can quantify how workload flexibility affects its system
impact in addition to its hosting capacity value. Finally, the
optimized workload schedules can support the design of flexi-
ble or non-firm connection arrangements by defining activation
conditions, workload service requirements, measurement and
verification procedures, and the settlement mechanisms. These
extensions would translate the quantified hosting capacity value
of DC workload flexibility into implementable planning and op-
erational solutions for power systems accommodating rapidly
growing AI-era DC demand.
